title: Samkhya (the 24 principles
hook: the Samkhya Karika begins the way a doctor does: there is pain, and the remedies on hand don't finish the job

segments.voice: Yesterday we said goodbye to Vaisheshika, atoms, with adrishta: the unseen left behind by what we do. What did you do well that nobody saw? A third school opens today. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-one.

A headache, again. You take something for it, and it works, for a while. Then it's back next week. A bad night of worry: you call a friend, it helps, and two nights later it's back. A storm takes out the power and there's nothing to do but wait. Some pain comes from inside us, some from other people, some from the weather and the world. And the fixes we keep in the drawer are real, but they don't finish the job. The text of today's school opens right there, the way a good doctor would, by asking what actually ends it.
screen: `THE HEADACHE COMES BACK.` → `THE FIXES IN THE DRAWER.` → `WHAT ACTUALLY ENDS IT?`

segments.voice: The school is Samkhya. Tradition names the sage Kapila as its source, and the text it's usually read through is a short book of verses, the Samkhya Karika. Its first verse says: because we are struck by three kinds of pain, we want to know what removes it. The commentators sort the three the way the hook did: pain from within, in body and mind; pain from other beings; and pain from forces beyond us. Then the Karika lets an objector speak. Why bother with philosophy? There's medicine. There are remedies. The answer is careful. It doesn't say medicine is bad. It says the seen remedies are not certain and not final. The pain returns. Then the second verse goes further. Even the rituals of the Veda, it says, are like the seen remedies. They help, but they come with flaws and they wear off. What is better, the verse says, is knowing. Knowing three things: what is manifest, what is unmanifest, and the knower. That's where the counting comes in. Some readers take the name Samkhya to mean counting, and others take it as discernment; either way, the school goes through reality item by item. Its third verse sorts everything into a root that comes from nothing else, things that come from it and give rise to more, and things that only come from others. Add them up and you have twenty-four principles of the world. And then there's one more, standing outside the count, that is neither made nor makes anything. We'll meet it tomorrow. For now, notice the move. Samkhya doesn't start with God or with atoms. It starts with pain, and with an honest question about what really ends it.
screen: `THREE KINDS OF PAIN.` · `SEEN REMEDIES DON'T FINISH IT.` · `KNOW THE WORLD, AND THE KNOWER.` · `TWENTY-FOUR, AND ONE MORE.` · then, large: `IT STARTS WITH PAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count, and then sort. Settle, and breathe. Count ten breaths, out and in, one to ten. If you lose count, start again at one; that's fine. Then bring to mind one pain you're carrying today, small or large. Ask which kind it is. Does it come from within, from your own body or mind? From another person? From the world, weather, news, circumstance? Just sort it. Don't fix it. Notice that something in you is able to look at the pain and name it. If you pray, you can hold that pain before God and keep breathing. The bell holds the time.
Samkhya. A school that begins with three kinds of pain, looks for what truly ends it, and counts out the world, twenty-four principles and one more.
Your line: Samkhya, the twenty-four principles. Today, when something hurts, sort it before you fix it: from within, from others, or from the world? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Samkhya is studied through the Samkhya Karika and its commentaries, and it is taught alongside Yoga, its paired school among the darshanas.

fork.setup: you're the objector in the Samkhya Karika. you say: "why study philosophy? there are remedies for pain." what does the text answer?
options: remedies are wrong, and you should give them up.
remedies help, but they aren't certain or final.
pain isn't real, so there's nothing to remedy.
fork.reveal: the Karika doesn't throw out medicine. it says the seen remedies aren't certain or final, and that knowing is better.

original.note: Sanskrit: Samkhya, the school whose name some take as counting, others as discernment.

trapdoor: what you thought: Samkhya is an abstract list of principles.
what it means: it starts with pain, like a doctor, and counts out the world to find what truly ends it.
what a scholar hears: Samkhya Karika 1–3: three kinds of pain; seen and Vedic remedies fall short; the root, the seven evolved-and-evolving, the sixteen evolved, and purusha, neither.

Index title/carry read 'Samkhya (the 24 principles' (closing parenthesis missing in the outline parse); kept exactly as the validator requires. The spoken carry says 'Samkhya, the twenty-four principles', matching day 1172.

'Twenty-four principles' is the sum of Karika 3's categories (1 root + 7 + 16), with purusha as the twenty-fifth; the verse itself gives 1, 7 and 16, not 24. Confirm the spoken phrasing 'add them up and you have twenty-four'.

Karika 1–2 paraphrased: duhkhatraya; seen means are aikanta/atyanta-less (not certain, not final); Vedic means are like the seen, with impurity, decay and excess; knowledge of vyakta, avyakta and jña is better. Confirm the gloss of the Vedic critique is fair and not framed as disrespect to the Veda.
The three kinds of pain (adhyatmika, adhibhautika, adhidaivika) as named by commentators (Gaudapada): confirm.
Kapila as source attributed to tradition; 'some readers' for the name meaning counting or discernment.
Day 1172 (another writer) introduces prakriti and purusha in detail; this day deliberately only previews 'one more, standing outside the count'.
howItsDone pairs Samkhya with Yoga among the darshanas; confirm phrasing.
